text.p: These are the key facts about the former Soviet republic of Belarus, which is locked in a political crisis over plans by President Alexander Lukashenko to increase his powers through a referendum on Sunday.
POPULATION: 10.25 million. An ethnic population breakdown from 1990 shows 77.9 percent Belarussians, 13.2 percent Russians, 4.1 percent Poles, 2.9 percent Ukrainians and 1.1 percent Jews.
AREA: 207,600 sq km (80,200 sq miles). Belarus borders Poland on the west with Lithuania and Latvia to the north and northwest. To the south lies Ukraine, to the east Russia.
CAPITAL: Minsk, population 1.6 million.

ECONOMY: Belarus, along with Ukraine and Russia, is one of the three "Slav heartland" republics which made up the core of the former Soviet Union. It was a key agricultural and technological base under Kremlin rule, but its industries have suffered greatly since independence in December 1991.
Its factories were noted for heavy-duty trucks, tractors, machine tools and agricultural machinery. But production has slumped sharply since independence.
Belarus is also a traditional producer of farm produce, especially potatoes and vegetables, sugar beet, flax and grain. Agriculture remains highly collectivised.

The republic's currency is the rouble, which has declined to around 2.60 to the Russian rouble since the two currencies were unlinked. Monthly inflation was 1.8 percent in September 1996. The economy is heavily indebted to Russia for energy supplies.
RELIGION: Mainly Russian Orthodox. Also large Roman Catholic and eastern rite Catholic communities.

LANGUAGE: Communist rule virtually drove into extinction the Belarussian language, an eastern Slav tongue similar to Russian and Ukrainian. Russian is spoken by most people. Only four percent of the population speak Belarussian regularly.

HISTORY: In its seven-century existence Belarus (which means "White Russia") has come mainly under the influence of its neighbours Poland and Russia, with no real experience of independent statehood before 1991.
During the upheavals of the 1917 Revolution the Belarussian National Convention proclaimed the country's independence for the first time.
But in 1919 Poland and Russia again divided the territory.
In 1939, the Nazi-Soviet pact dismembering Poland meant that the Soviet Union could claim the whole of Belarus for itself.
But when Germany attacked the USSR in 1941, Belarus was overrun. During the Nazi occupation 25 percent of the population died. Industry and agriculture were destroyed.

Post-war reconstruction put the republic into the forefront of Soviet production. It became one of the most hardline republics, heralding a long period of Russification. The Belarussian Communist Party, dominated by a group of former World War Two anti-Nazi partisans, was a slavish follower of Moscow.
Although it was given a seat of its own in the U.N., along with Ukraine, Belarus never stepped out of line with Moscow.
Known as the "quiet republic," Belarus hardly stirred during the first years of Mikhail Gorbachev's perestroika reforms.
But the 1986 explosion at Ukraine's Chernobyl nuclear station affected Belarus most and set off a political reaction.
Authorities tried to cover up the extent of the disaster but later admitted a third of Belarus was contaminated.
The Belarussian Popular Front (BPF), an opposition group, capitalised on the disaster to stage large demonstrations.
In July 1990, the Belarussian parliament followed in the footsteps of Ukraine, Moldova and the three Baltic republics by declaring its sovereignty.
The failed August 1991 Kremlin coup and the imminent collapse of Soviet power saw a surge in nationalist sentiment. But unlike Ukraine and other republics, Belarus never sought independence actively.

Stanislav Shushkevich, a professor outside the top ranks of the Communist Party, became head of state and hosted the December 1991 meeting with the leaders of Ukraine and Russia at Belovezhskaya Pushcha near Brest which proclaimed the end of the Soviet Union. Large numbers of Russian troops remained, though Belarus agreed to get rid of its nuclear weapons.
Shushkevich's attempts to introduce reforms met resistance from conservatives and he was ousted as chairman of parliament in January 1994.

In July 1994 a presidential election was won by a maverick outsider and anti-corruption campaigner, Alexander Lukashenko. Since his election he has won a May 1995 referendum to restore the symbols and flag of the Soviet era, and tried to reunite his country with Russia, playing on nostalgia for the Soviet Union and pro-Russian sentiments among a population whose sense of national identity is weak.
Under Lukashenko state control of the economy has been restored, relations with the West have cooled sharply and most Western financial institutions have halted aid.

Independent trade unions have been banned, demonstrators have been jailed and newspaper editors sacked, while Lukashenko has often ignored rulings against him by the constitutional court. Leaders of the nationalist opposition have been given political asylum in the United States.
Belarus is the only European state outside former Yugoslavia which has yet to join the Council of Europe.
